title: A Peg in Plain Sight
blurb: The unbeaten Tannery Hounds throw notes no pair can null, so Kilnyard leaves the Dead Air on the shelf and bets everything on a peg in plain sight.

blocks.text: The first note doesn't arrive. It leans in.

It's so low I get it in my teeth before my ear. A rattle in the back molars, then a buzz up through my bare soles, then all six plates on our wall start humming along, the way a shelf of pans answers a dropped lid. The front of it glows wide and dull, a lamp behind a sheet.
The Tannery Hounds don't throw notes. They throw weather.

That one was six paces long. No pair on any floor in Caddrow can kill a note longer than five. So tonight the Dead Air is useless, and every note that reaches me goes into my body, and into the Book for good.
It's only the warm-up. Thunder, clearing his throat.
Nobody has said the word Chapterhouse in six days.

We say Round 9. We say it the way people say "his chest" about a man who's dying. Since the letter, Quist has come to every drill night and coached like a man driving fence posts before the ground freezes.
Tonight he's followed us down the Tannery stair and stopped on the bottom step, boots on. Away floor. Not his. It smells of lime pits and wet hide, and the walls sweat.
I go to him while the others strip their boots. I stand where he can see my mouth.
"Are we going?" I say. "Round 9."
"Custom," Quist says. "Can't refuse. Forfeit."
"And if we play the Dead Air on their floor?"
He looks at me a long time. His fingers find the stair rail. Tap. Tap-tap. Rest.
"Then they watch," he says.
"They watched you."
"Aye." Tap. Tap-tap. "Then stopped watching. Started doing." He leans in, too loud, the way he always is. "Not you, lad. Not with a gallery. Not twice."
He doesn't sound sure. He sounds like a man setting a stone he hasn't tested.

I don't tell him what I'm thinking, which is this. The Chapter's floor is old. And if it's like ours, if something under it answers a clean Dead Air the way something under Kilnyard answers mine, then the Chapter will be standing right on top of it with their listening rods, and I'll be the one knocking.
I still haven't told Quist what our floor does. I don't tell him tonight either.

Sef turns up at my right side. He always picks the right one now. "Two things," he says. "One, if we lose tonight, Round 9 decides nothing and the Chapter can keep its floor. Two. No, three. Two, the Hounds are unbeaten. Three, Thunder and Worse are both too long to null, so tonight we couldn't show the Chapter a Dead Air if we wanted to."
"Good," Quist says. He's read every word of it off Sef's mouth. "Win without it. Learn that."
"How?" Dov says from the floor, one boot off. "Respectfully. How?"
Quist points. At me. At Marten. Then he holds up one finger at Oduya, which is more respect than I've seen him give anyone.
"Ordinary Quells. Few as you can." He nods at her. "And her."
So Sef names Oduya to the Warden as Tuner and leaves the second Calling stand empty. Dov Calls alone. The Dead Air goes on the shelf with every other tool I own that's no use on this job.

I tap the walls before the first Raise. Cold, wet and even, all the way round. Damp slows a Drum and shortens the waves, but not by enough. If this one sagged a whole half-pace, Thunder's six would still come in over five. The Warden swings his tell-weight and calls pace five. He's honest. It doesn't help.
Oduya stands at our plate rail with her hand on the Last Plate's pitch peg, like a woman at a stove with her hand on the pot.
"Tell me again," Dov says. "Slowly. Like I'm a Caller."

"Thunder's voice is a stockpot, Dov Carrick," Oduya says. "It is happiest at one heat. Worse is a larger pot that sits a little lower. At every Breath I move our plate one semitone down, to a note in the speaking scale that sits between their two heats. Neither of them can hold it without bending, and bending boils a voice dry."
"And they'll see you do it."
"Everybody will see me do it. That is what a peg is for."

The Tannery Scribe is a small, neat man with a belt buckle the size of a saucer. Sef has already called him Buckle twice. At the first Breath Oduya moves the peg, and Buckle's eyes go straight to our rail, and he says something short to his Callers, and Thunder shifts his weight.

Thunder throws first. Weight 3, straight down the middle. I stand in the line and let it go through me, which is like being leaned on by a carthorse. It loses a weight in me and still rings our Last Plate for three counts. One to them.
Dov answers with the Lamplighter. One-one.
Second Breath. Oduya moves the peg again. Buckle reads it and frowns. Worse throws, bends to chase it, and the plate rattles. Nothing.
Third Breath. One more semitone down.
I feel it in my soles before Thunder's lead-in has crossed half the floor. His hum sits right on the peg. Right in the middle of it.
"Oduya," I say.
"I see it." Quietly. "I've walked it straight through his kitchen."
Thunder voices hard. Weight 4. It isn't coming at me; it's coming down the far line, and nobody's on it but the Last Stand, and Marten's on the Last Stand, empty, hands at his sides.

The note hits our Last Plate within a quarter-tone. The plate doesn't ring. It sings. You can hear the difference from the stair. A Peal is three counts. A hard note that close keeps going to six, and six is three points.
One count.
Marten doesn't look at Sef. He doesn't wait for a call. He turns on the Last Stand and puts both palms flat on the singing brass.
Two.
It stops.

I've never watched a Hand-Still from close. It doesn't look like anything. A man leaning on a door. Then Marten's knees go, a little, and he locks them, and the Warden's lantern on the hook goes up bright and yellow.
The Warden sets his rod's foot on the Last Stand. "Eight held," he says. Then, louder, to the scorer on the gallery: "Thirty-nine, Sallow."
Marten watches the Warden's mouth until it shuts. Then he nods.

Eight is the line. Lit at eight, you're withdrawn for the Half at once, no Breaths, no argument. Marten steps off the stand by himself and walks to our bench with his hands held out in front of him like they're wet.
"I'd have called it," Sef says, low.
"Aye, well," Marten says. "You'd have been slower."
He sits. He starts humming, out of habit, one of his lullabies, to a bench that isn't a floor.
Thirty-nine. One Mark from Rung Out. He's saved us three points and spent the last of himself doing it.

Jory comes down off the reserves' step at the next Breath, sleeves sooty, chin up. She's registered as a Caller. She can't draw. Nobody can do anything about that until the Half, so for the rest of it there's one Damper on our side of the Drum, and it's me.
"Two things," Sef says. "One, Wren draws nothing unless I say so. Two, Jory, you're a wall now."
"I'm a what?"
"Stand where I point and be heavy."
She stands where he points. Worse's next hard note knocks her clean off her stand, and she steps straight back on, white-faced, and stays there.

Oduya keeps walking the peg. Down a semitone. Down another. Buckle reads every move and mutters, and every time his Callers find the pitch, the pitch has already gone. Worse bends onto it once and Peals: two-one. Dov answers with the Counterfeit, and then, two throws later, Jory throws her first Caller's note of the night, a thin bright thing nobody's watching, and it rings Tannery's Last Plate for three counts.
"The Sootlight again," Dov shouts. "Hers! Nobody else's!"
At the Half it's three-two to us. My hands are clean. So far.
The Long Ground clears every ring in the Drum. It doesn't clear Marten's Book.
"You sit," Sef tells him. "One Mark off. You don't stand."
"Aye, well."
Sef registers Dov as a Damper and Jory to Call. Dov goes the colour of tallow. He doesn't go near a bucket.
"I'm fine," he says. "I'm the Widowmaker of fine."

Oduya's peg is home now: six semitones down from rest, as far as the rule allows, on a note no sporting scale has a name for. It sits in the crack between Thunder's heat and Worse's like a coin down the back of a settle.

Buckle has one answer and he uses it. Worse bends. Every throw, up onto our peg, two semitones, at double the cost. It works. Tannery Peal twice, and I can hear it costing him: by the second, his voice is wearing through like a boot heel. Jory Peals once, a low curving thing that Dov names from his Damper's stand before it's stopped ringing.
"The Lime Pit!"
Four-four.
Their last throw of the Half is the last throw of regulation. Twelfth. Theirs.
Buckle doesn't send one Caller. He sends both.

A chord. Thunder and Worse side by side, one beam, two pitches. I get both lead-ins through my feet at once, the way you feel two carts on one road. One sits a semitone above Oduya's peg. One sits a semitone below.
Within a semitone is a Peal. Either pitch lands, it rings. Buckle has stopped trying to hit the peg. He's straddled it.

The beam is three paces wide and it covers one stand on our side. Mine. Dov's outside it. Jory's outside it. It's coming down the line to me and through me to the plate, and if I let it through it loses a weight in me and rings anyway, and Tannery win.
Neither pitch can be nulled. Neither one is short enough. No pair on any floor.
I don't wait for Sef. I don't need to. I watch him nod.
Palms out. Breath in.
The front comes. I draw.

Weight 3 lands like a sack of wet sand on the breastbone. Weight 2 comes in behind it, a half-beat flatter, and settles lower, in the hips. Both of them go down into me and stay. My ears ring. My hands go, both of them, from the fingertips back, until it's like holding two lumps of cold mortar on the ends of my arms.
Our Last Plate stays dark.
The Warden comes and sets his rod on my stand. He listens.
"Five held," he says. Then up to the gallery: "Seven, Halloway."
Seven. Two more Marks in the Book, and the Book doesn't give back.
The lantern on my hook stays dark. Five isn't lit. Five is the last number before it.
"Four-four," the Warden says. "Sudden Peal. Tannery throw."
Hob Rennie stood at five.

I wasn't there. I've heard it from everyone who was. A pre-season friendly, a Damper at five held ring, a weight-five note coming at him alone, and his Scribe shouting him off it. He drew it anyway. Ten. Rung Out on the spot, for life, on a night that didn't count.
His Scribe was Sef.
Sef is looking at me now with a face I haven't seen on him. Not the clever one.
The Breath is three counts. I should be Grounding it. Feet planted, hum down, one ring out. I'm not, because Sef has me moving.

"Last Stand," he says. "Now. Dov, there. Jory, there. Oduya, off the rail, there." He points at three stands in a line across Thunder's straight path, between Thunder and me. Three bodies. "They've thrown straight all night. They'll throw straight now."
I cross the floor on feet I can barely feel and step up onto the Last Stand.
"Halloway." Sef is at my right shoulder. "You draw nothing. Whatever comes. Not if it's a weight one."
"And if my hands go anyway?"
He swallows. "Then they go on a two."
"Thunder's best is a five," he says, fast. "Through three of us a five comes out a two. You draw a two, you're lit. You're not Rung Out."
That's what the three of them are standing in a line for. Not the plate. Me. In case I'm Hob.
I put my hands down at my sides. They don't feel like mine. I leave them there.
The Warden's tell-weight swings. Thunder lifts a hand.
He hasn't got Worse's voice to lean on. Worse is spent, hoarse, standing behind him with a hand on his own throat. It's Thunder alone, and Thunder's voice is a stockpot, and Oduya has moved the heat.
His lead-in comes through the floor. Into my soles. Through numb hands that still know which way is down.
Off the peg. Sharp of it, reaching down for a note his throat won't go to. Not a little.
A semitone and a half.

It isn't going to Peal. My feet know it before anybody's ears do. My hands want to come up anyway, the way your hand goes out when you trip on a stair. I keep them where they are. I keep them there because Sef said so and because three people are standing in front of me so that I can.
Thunder voices.

It hits Dov first and he rocks and stays on. It hits Jory and knocks her off her stand, and she climbs straight back on, furious. It hits Oduya, who sways like a tall pot on a trivet and doesn't spill. Then it hits me at weight two, and I don't draw, and it shoves through me like a door opening, and strikes our Last Plate.
The plate rattles. A cheap, tinny buzz, like a spoon in a drawer.
Nothing.
The gallery goes silent.

At the Breath I Ground. Heels, then balls, bedding myself into the stand, one low hum straight down into a floor that has nobody under it. One ring out. Then Jory lifts her hand to Raise, and our side is throwing, and one more goes.

She hums her lead-in the way she copied Dov's from the kiln stair, quiet, settling it, eyes on Tannery's peg. Tannery carry no Tuner. Their peg has sat at rest all night, in plain sight, and she's had two Halves to look at it. She voices high and clean and dead on it.
Their Last Plate rings. One. Two. Three.
Five-four.
The Tannery Hounds have lost a match.
Dov doesn't name it. He opens his mouth and nothing comes out, and then he sits down on his Damper's stand and laughs until he has to wipe his face.
"That one doesn't get a name," he says, when he can. "That one gets a statue."
The gallery empties slowly. Buckle shakes Sef's hand and doesn't let go of it for a while. The others go up the stair singing something rude about lime pits, Jory loudest.
I stay to Ground the last of it out. A copy floor. Nothing underneath. Just stone, and my hum going into it and stopping, which tonight is exactly what I want from stone.
Marten comes down off the bench and stands on the stand beside mine. The Long Ground cleared him hours ago. He hums anyway. The lullaby.
"Round 9," he says. "That's my last."
I look at him.

"Thirty-nine," he says. "I'll stand at the Chapterhouse, and I'll walk off it on my own feet, and that's me. My girls want a dad with hands." He nods at the Last Stand behind us. "And you'll be on that."
"I stood on it for one throw tonight and kept my hands at my sides. That's not playing it."
"Aye, well. You will."
I bend down for my boots. With my face in the dark under the bench, I say, "Then who partners me?"
Nothing. He goes on humming.
I straighten up with the boots in my hand. He's watching me, patient, waiting for me to speak. So I say it again, facing him. "Who partners me?"
"I do," he says, straight off. "Last one."

He didn't ignore the first one. He never had it. Marten Sallow, my partner, the man whose draw has to land in the same instant as mine, has been reading every word I've said to him this season off my mouth. He hardly hears my voice at all.
